title: Cameron, Colorado
author: Aaron Walton
quote: the Cameron town site was the location of a small ranching community that was known as Grassy ... In 1899 a development company purchased the townsite and laid out the town of Cameron. A post office was established in 1901. ... Located south of town, this 30 acre park became the most popular recreation spot in the entire district. ... In 1909 the post office was closed. [Atlas note, not the source's words: Names no sources. Its statement that 'In 1892 a railroad depot was established here' is two years before the railway is said to have reached Gillett. Its map link is 38.746651, -105.099061, which is on Beaver Creek about 1.9 miles east of the point used here: see the place's open questions.]

title: Pinnacle Park (photograph 001-5301): catalogue description
holder: Pikes Peak Library District, Margaretta M. Boas Photograph Collection
quote: Pinnacle Park, an amusement park near Cameron, Colorado, was built by the Woods Investment Company in 1900. The park was located on either side of parallel Colorado Midland Terminal and Short Line tracks. A rustic bridge spanned the tracks and offered visitors easy access to both sections of the park.

title: The Cripple Creek Times (illustrated New Year edition in book form)
holder: Library of Congress copy, on the Internet Archive (cripplecreektime00crip)
quote: As Cameron, the first town touched in the district, is reached, the Victor and the Isabella properties, two of the big mines of Bull hill, are in view. At Cameron the lines of the road diverge. One branch leads to the right, crossing over Hoosier pass at an altitude of 10,360 feet. ... The other branch of the main line turns to the left at Cameron and passes through Pinnacle park, and the flourishing mining towns of Independence and Goldfield, over Victor pass, and has its terminus in Victor. ... The Short Line railroad has planned to locate its shops at this point. Pinnacle Park, the breathing place of the district, is at Cameron. [Atlas note, not the source's words: read from the Internet Archive's text of the scan, with its line-break hyphens closed up and 'Hoosler' read as Hoosier; the passage describes the Short Line. A search of the text found no picture captioned Cameron or Pinnacle Park, and only six of the 166 pages were looked at.]
